title: Observability and Data
content:
The Grafana LGTM stack, cloud-agnostic architecture, and the analytics that sit on both.
Observability Deep experience, and deliberately weighted toward open source datasources. A vendor-neutral stack is easier to operate, cheaper at volume, and it does not turn a licensing change into an incident. Search terms: monitoring, logging, tracing, dashboards, alerting, uptime, outage detection, cost control.
Metrics Prometheus: exposition, recording and alerting rules, remote write, and the cardinality budget treated as a cost rather than an afterthought Mimir: long-term storage, multi-tenant federation, and running metrics at a scale where a single Prometheus is no longer the answer Relabelling at collection: keeping high-cardinality dimensions out of the TSDB instead of dropping them in the query Metrics that mean something: SLI definitions agreed with the business before the dashboard is built, not inferred from whatever was already instrumented
Logs Loki: label design, index cost, retention policies, and the discipline of structured logging that makes querying possible at all Querying logs at scale: LogQL, query splitting, and knowing when to go to the datasource instead of pushing a broad query at it Routing by signal: separating what needs full-text search from what only needs to be counted, and pricing the difference
Traces Tempo: distributed tracing, traceQL, and the sampling decisions that determine whether a trace is useful or merely expensive OpenTelemetry instrumentation: SDK configuration, context propagation across async boundaries, and auto-instrumentation where it earns its keep versus where it hides the interesting call Connecting the three: exemplars and trace-to-logs from Grafana, so a spike in an error rate leads to the exact trace and then the exact log line without leaving one screen
Dashboards and alerting Grafana: provisioning as code, folders as ownership boundaries, data sources declared in version control, and alert rules that live with the service they watch SLOs and burn-rate alerting: error budgets as a shared language, and alerts that page on symptoms a human cares about rather than on every metric that moved Dashboards that get read: few, opinionated, and built around a question rather than around available data
Operating the stack Single-tenant and high-availability deployment: replicated datasources, object storage backed retention, and a configuration that survives losing a zone Capacity planning: ingestion growth, retention cost, and sharding thresholds known before they are hit Cost discipline: the observability bill is usually the fastest-growing line in an infrastructure budget, and cardinality and retention are where it goes Performance telemetry: continuous profiling, and capacity forecasting from real usage rather than from a spreadsheet
Cloud-Agnostic Architecture Building systems that are not hostage to one provider, so a price change, a retired product, or a bad week in one region is a procurement decision rather than an incident. Search terms: multi-cloud, hybrid cloud, private cloud, vendor lock-in, portability, exit strategy.
Provider primitives without provider shape: designing against AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure APIs while keeping the dependencies that matter behind an interface OpenStack and private cloud: on-premises and sovereign deployments, where portability is a hard requirement and egress is metered Multi-cloud networking: private interconnects, transit gateways, DNS management, and egress control Hybrid patterns: burst capacity, data locality, and an explicit exit strategy for every external dependency Storage portability: object storage semantics, replication across providers, and the restore path being tested rather than assumed Identity across clouds: federation, per-cloud IAM boundaries, and short-lived credentials as the default rather than the exception Cost portability: knowing which parts of the architecture are genuinely portable and which are a deliberate bet on one provider
Data and Analytics The analytics side sits deliberately next to the platform side. The same people who build and run the datasources are the ones who query them, which means a question about production data gets answered by whoever built the path to it rather than by a handoff. Search terms: reporting, business intelligence, forecasting, prediction, machine learning, data pipeline.
Operational data first This is the work we are deepest in, because the data already exists and the problems are well understood.
Natural-language querying: a question in English producing PromQL, LogQL, or SQL against the observability stack, scoped read-only, with the generated query shown so the answer can be checked rather than trusted Anomaly detection on telemetry: baselines and drift detection over metrics and logs, with the false-positive rate measured instead of assumed, because an alert nobody trusts is an alert nobody reads Capacity forecasting: projecting growth in ingestion, storage, and node counts to size them before the incident rather than during it Cardinality and cost analysis: finding the label or metric responsible for an observability bill that grew without anyone deciding it should Window functions and query tuning: the unglamorous work of making a query over a year of logs finish in seconds, with the plan explained Dashboards as answers: a small number of views built around a question someone actually asks, rather than around whatever happened to be instrumented
Modelling and machine learning Classical modelling: regression, classification, clustering, and time-series forecasting, with the baseline established first so there is something to beat Feature engineering from operational data: turning metrics, logs, and deployment history into features, and knowing which of them are leakage Model serving: packaging a trained model behind a service, versioning it, and rolling it forward without a redeploy Model monitoring: drift and degradation detection in production, which is a different discipline from detecting drift in a notebook Evaluation that survives contact with reality: a holdout that reflects the production distribution, metrics chosen for the decision rather than for the paper, and a stated threshold for when a model is not worth running The honest part: knowing when a rule or a query is the right answer and a model is not. Most operational problems do not need one, and we say so
Pipelines and tooling Python: pandas, Polars, and Arrow for anything larger than fits in memory, with chunked and out-of-core processing rather than a machine with more RAM Data storage: Parquet, columnar formats, partitioning, and compression chosen for how the data is actually read Workflow orchestration: Airflow for dependencies, retries, backfills, and the scheduling that keeps a dataset honest about when it is current Notebooks and reproducibility: analysis as versioned code that runs later, not as a file whose output nobody can regenerate Data quality: contracts, freshness and volume checks, and failing a pipeline on bad input instead of publishing it
Data stores and messaging PostgreSQL: query plans and reading EXPLAIN, indexing strategy, replication topology, failover, connection pooling, and vacuum behaviour under write pressure MySQL and MariaDB: replication topology, binlog handling, and upgrade procedures that keep a rolling fleet consistent MongoDB: aggregation pipelines, sharding, and the schema decisions that make sharding possible or impossible later Elasticsearch and OpenSearch: index lifecycle, mapping and query design, and the operational cost of a cluster that has to stay up Redis: persistence and eviction policy as capacity decisions, cluster topology, and cache stampede protection RabbitMQ: exchange types, queues, and dead-letter handling for workflows that must not silently drop work
Where the two meet The most useful work happens in the overlap. Operational data is high-volume, messy, and genuinely interesting, and the models that pay for themselves are usually about the system you run rather than about a customer in a spreadsheet: capacity, failure prediction, and cost.
